Research and learning · interactive reader

Consistent hashing, in one ring

See why a changing cache fleet can move only the keys owned by one small arc instead of remapping almost everything.

Three principles

The model before the mechanism

1

Wrap the hash space

Map nodes and keys onto the same circle. Values after the maximum continue at zero, so there is always a next position.

2

Walk clockwise

Each key belongs to the first node clockwise from its position. Labels and square keys keep ownership readable without color alone.

3

Move one arc

When a node leaves or joins, only keys in the affected neighboring arc change owners. Other assignments stay stable.

Worked example

Four nodes, thirty-two keys, one fleet change

Modulo hashing

Changing from four nodes to five changes the divisor. Roughly four out of five keys receive a different remainder and move.

Consistent hashing

Adding one position gives the new node only its predecessor’s arc. Roughly one out of five keys moves; other assignments remain stable.

Transient simulation

Change the ring

Adjust the bounded controls or use the node buttons. Reloading restores four nodes and thirty-two keys.

  • Nlabeled circle: node
  • ◆square: key

4 nodes and 32 keys. Ready.

Operational scenarios

What changes—and what does not

Node loss

The removed node’s keys move clockwise to its successor. Keys owned by every other node retain the same owner.

Watch: the moved count changes while most square markers keep their label and position.

Scale out

The added node takes the arc immediately before its deterministic ring position.

Watch: only keys in that arc transfer; the new node never forces a whole-ring reshuffle.

Production systems use many virtual nodes per server. This reader keeps one position per node so the ownership rule stays visible.
